reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Bowen
bases: A party took Bowen from the Union Bridge lockup, put a noose on his neck at a tree and tried to hang him for an alleged assault; he escaped (A2, A5, A21).

A group of twelve or more broke into the lockup and tried to hang Bowen as punishment for an alleged assault, but he escaped alive (A2, A5, A21); early reports that he was hanged (A1) were overtaken by his recapture and trial (A14, A22), so this was an attempted lynching.

The local Democratic Advocate (A5, A21), a Baltimore German paper (A11) and the wire dispatches (A2, A14) agree that Bowen was taken from the lockup, noosed and escaped; only the first dispatch (A1) said he was killed, and details of the mob are disputed by Bowen (A21).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of John Bowen took place at Union Bridge, Carroll County, Maryland, early on June 15, 1888, when a party took Bowen, a Black man held for cutting two Black people with a razor, from the town lockup and tried to hang him.
Bowen slipped the noose, was recaptured about a week later and was convicted of assault with intent to kill in December.
Wire reports noted that the lynchers were Black men, though Bowen later said most of the crowd was white.

According to the Westminster Democratic Advocate, on Wednesday night, June 13, Bowen attacked Otho Jones, a blind man, and Ida Milbury, both Black, on their way home from Union Bridge, after she refused to go with him.
He was said to have broken her jaw and nearly severed her ears with a razor and to have cut Jones nine times.
A widely reprinted dispatch gave the motive as jealousy and said Bowen had served a year in the penitentiary for assaulting a Miss Taylor of the town.
He was arrested on Thursday night when he returned by train from Westminster, where, he later said, he had consulted his lawyer about giving bail.
About one o'clock on Friday morning a party broke into the lockup, carried Bowen to an oak tree on the edge of town and put a noose around his neck.
The wire dispatch said twelve or fifteen "colored men, all masked" slackened the rope when he motioned to speak, and fired after him without effect when he slipped it and ran.
The Democratic Advocate said instead that the rope proved too short and he leaped away while it was being lengthened.
Constable Repp's search party failed to find him, and residents who feared his revenge formed a volunteer police force, according to Baltimore's Der Deutsche Correspondent.
Deputy Sheriff Tyler tracked him to near Greencastle, Pennsylvania, and found him sitting on a fence; Bowen offered no resistance and asked for protection.
He was lodged in the Westminster jail; a crowd met the train but made no demonstration.
In a jail interview reprinted by the Democratic Advocate, Bowen denied the assault, whose victims had by then recovered.
He said the girl's father, "Old man Milbury," carried the rope, with "two or three 'coons' and a large crowd of whites," and he gave his lawyer their names but would not make them public.
No report of arrests of the lynchers was found.
On December 4 a Westminster jury deliberated five hours and found Bowen guilty on both charges of assault with intent to kill; no report of his sentence was found.
The first dispatches split on the outcome.

Under the headline "Colored Men Lynch a Colored Man," the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer said Bowen had been hanged by men of his "own race," the fourth lynching in Carroll County in two years, and papers in Maysville and Washington repeated it.

The escape version ran the same day in the Alexandria Gazette and the Washington Evening Star and on June 16 in the New-York Tribune, the Richmond Dispatch and the St. Paul Daily Globe; weeklies as far as Kansas and Georgia reprinted it into late June.

Headlines dwelt on the escape and Bowen's character: "A Bold Dash for Life" and "Negro Desperado" in the Tribune, "A Colored Brute Escapes Lynching" in St. Paul, and "Judge Lynch Fooled" in Emporia, whose subhead called him a "Coon."
No paper criticized the lynchers, and the Catoctin Clarion described his escape "at the hands of colored citizens."
The Democratic Advocate also called Bowen a "Colored Desperado," yet it alone printed his account, in which he called his would-be killers guiltier than himself.
The wire, the local paper and the German paper described the mob as Black men, while Bowen said a few Black men acted with a large crowd of whites.
Bowen also said he was never lifted off his feet and denied the story that he asked time to pray, and reports put his capture on June 23 or 24.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch (Union Bridge, June 15)
accounts.gist: Twelve or fifteen masked Black men took Bowen from jail and strung him up; he motioned to speak, slipped the slackened rope and fled under fire.

accounts.label: Early dispatch (completed-lynching version)
accounts.gist: Bowen was taken 200 yards from town and hanged to an oak by men of his own race.

accounts.label: Democratic Advocate, local first report
accounts.gist: A crowd of Black men broke into the lockup; the rope was too short and Bowen leaped away while it was being lengthened.

accounts.label: Der Deutsche Correspondent
accounts.gist: Twelve to fifteen of his own race took him quietly; he got the noose loosened by offering to confess and fled to the woods.

accounts.label: Bowen's jail interview
accounts.gist: Old man Milbury had the rope, with two or three Black men and a large crowd of whites; they never lifted him off his feet; he slipped his thumbs under the noose and ran; he denied the assault.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Union Bridge wire as an escape story under headlines such as 'He Fooled the Lynchers' and 'A Bold Dash for Life', calling Bowen a 'Negro Desperado'.
The first dispatch, 'Colored Men Lynch a Colored Man', emphasized that the lynchers were of Bowen's own race and reported him dead.
Western reprints used contemptuous headlines: 'A Colored Brute Escapes Lynching' and 'Judge Lynch Fooled. A Masked Party Let a Coon Slip Through Their Fingers'.
The local Democratic Advocate headlined Bowen a 'Colored Desperado' but later printed his long interview accusing a white crowd and calling the lynchers guiltier than himself.

versions.value: Bowen escaped the noose and was later recaptured

conflicts.note: The escape version is confirmed by the recapture, the jail interview and the December trial; the 'lynched' report was an early error (the Democratic Advocate notes a rumor that he had been hanged and buried).

Union Bridge, Md.: taken from the town lockup to an oak tree on the outskirts, in a field belonging to Granville Haines (per Bowen)
John Bowen, colored (printed Bowens, Bowans, Rowans, Swans); survived

Accused of assaulting with a razor Otho Jones, a blind Black man, and Ida Milbury (Milberry, Mulberry, Hollenberry), a Black girl or woman, on Wednesday night, June 13, after she refused to go with him; charged with assault with intent to kill. Bowen denied it.
Contested: 'colored men, all masked' (wire, local paper) versus Bowen's claim of the girl's father, two or three Black men and a large crowd of whites, unmasked at first
Bowen escaped the lynching, was recaptured and jailed at Westminster, and was convicted in December
